Sampled HR@K measures success against sampled candidates; it can reverse model rankings relative to full-catalog HR@K, even in expectation. Repeating negative sampling quantifies candidate randomness but cannot eliminate this bias. Krichene and Rendle demonstrate the distinction and discuss corrections with bias–variance tradeoffs. For this benchmark, retain its pinned sampled HR@10 as the selection objective; additional sampling would be a separate diagnostic. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651).

A practical synthesis: evaluate both models on identical users and identical negative sets for every repetition; record paired hit differences d(u,r). With candidates fixed, bootstrap users within each category, carrying each user’s paired observations together, then average the four category means equally. This estimates user variability conditional on those candidates. Cluster bootstrap methods preserve repeated observations within subjects; paired resampling preserves correspondence between models. [ClusterBootstrap](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7148287/), [SciPy bootstrap](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html).

To isolate candidate variability, hold users and trained models fixed and regenerate independent candidate sets under the same sampling rules, sharing each set across models. Report the standard deviation of paired macro-HR differences across repetitions; its standard error divided by √R describes Monte Carlo uncertainty of their average. User-cluster bootstrapping of per-user repetition averages estimates user uncertainty with reduced candidate noise. These are proposed procedures synthesized from the sources, not a specific published recommender protocol. Repeated candidate draws are dependent through users and must not be treated as additional independent users; neither procedure captures training-seed variability or adaptive model-selection uncertainty.
